newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden FinMin says public opinon swayed EMU view.
newsitem.headline: Sweden FinMin says public opinon swayed EMU view.

text.p: Sweden's Finance Minister Erik Asbrink on Wednesday said the ruling Social Democrats might have chosen to join Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) at the start in 1999 if Swedes had supported the project.

"If the public opinion was strongly in favour that would have been a decisive element," Asbrink said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television (RFTV). "Maybe that would have changed our action."

The Social Democratic party board announced on Tuesday that it did not want Sweden to join EMU in 1999 because the single currency looked too shaky and public opinion was too negative, but they wanted the door kept open for a future link.

A survey by pollster Skop published last week showed around 30 percent of the population were against EMU, while 35 percent preferred to wait and see, 21 percent wanted Sweden to join in 1999 and the rest were undecided.
Asbrink said Swedes' negative view on EMU was linked to hostility against the European Union (EU) which they, wrongly, connected with the budget cutbacks in Sweden.
It was important to change public opinion on the EU, which in turn would influence views on monetary union, he said.

"With the consolidation of public finances, which has come far in Sweden, and with the economic recovery, I think the general sentiment will be turning gradually into a more positive direction," he said.
Although Asbrink said Sweden intended to implement strict fiscal discipline he admitted that staying outside meant other options to smooth out fluctuations in the economy.
"When you have a single currency you eliminate some of the mechanisms that could be used to smooth out differences between the economies," he told RFTV.
"In that case (of a single currency) one has to rely on other mechanisms so there is a risk involved.
"But I think there is a good chance that the project will be a success and if that is the case that could certainly influence public opinion in Sweden."
Despite the government's freedom to step in and smooth out such differences, Asbrink said the Social Democrats EMU decision would not necessarily push interest rates higher.
"It's possible that a country like Sweden has to pay a certain price (for staying outside EMU) -- maybe we are paying that price already today," he said.
"On the other hand, in the longer perspective interest rates are decided by the development of the economy and economic policies."
Therefore it is not impossible that the long bond yield spread to Germany, which stood at 108 basis points at 1055 GMT, will narrow, he said.
Sweden's economy has improved significantly in the past couple of years and fundamentals are strong with a low inflation and large current account surplus.
